verdict.reasoning: Patient states left arm is numb with tingling that has worsened over time: “I can't quite move my left arm… it's numb, and then I also feel some, like tingling in my fingertips… it's probably been… at least two weeks, and it's kind of gotten worse… then the numbing kind of started.”

Transcript: “I've been taking this boxing class for a few weeks… It's probably been, I'd say, for at least two weeks, and it's kind of gotten worse.” This indicates symptoms have been present for at least two weeks during the period of boxing, not that they began two weeks *after* starting boxing class.

Patient: “I can feel it both in my… elbow, and then in my arm, as well as in my hand… it's my second, third, and fourth finger… it's… the front side.” She also reports intermittent shoulder pain with movement: “sometimes I will feel it in my shoulder… if I try to… move like in boxing… maybe feel a little bit of… pain.”

Patient notes functional difficulty: “I play a little bit of a piano and so I just noticed it's been kind of harder to get the notes.” Doctor clarifies weakness vs pain, and patient agrees it is numbness/weakness: “So you would say it's definitely weakness…?” Patient: “No, no, it's not hurting… it's, like, numb, I can't feel it.”

Patient: “I tried to get a massage, it's not better. Or, you know, try to take warm baths. It's not better… I do take Ibuprofen because my muscles were sore… But… that didn't help with this numbness thing.”

Patient: “I all of a sudden just couldn't see from… my left eye… I lost some… field of vision… that just lasted maybe for, I don't know, twenty, twenty minutes?” and later confirms: “I think it was only maybe like twenty minutes or so.” She says this was “a few weeks ago.”

Patient: “I also had a really bad cold, like a month ago… we were like out partying until… late hours, and I just got uncharacteristically drunk… And then after that, I was sick for probably good like two weeks… I think I must have had some kind of like a flu or something.” This supports a severe flu‑like illness after heavy alcohol consumption about a month ago.

Headaches: “Sometimes I get headaches but I think they're just tired headaches.” Fatigue: “I work too much… I'll go for a workout and then I'll really just exhaust myself and then I just kind of feel this fatigue… like this morning… I just felt really, fatigued and I couldn't even get myself to the gym.” These are consistent with intermittent fatigue and tension‑type (tired) headaches.

When asked about past medical history, patient mainly describes recent illnesses and then states: “but in general, I'm, I'm pretty healthy… I don't really have any medical problems.” No chronic past medical conditions are reported.

Patient: “I do take Ibuprofen… Not really [regular meds]. I just take ibuprofen every once in a while, I take vitamin D. Um, I take some… iron supplements, but… most of the time I just forget… And then, sometimes I take Melatonin to help me sleep.” This matches ibuprofen PRN, vitamin D, intermittent iron, and PRN melatonin.
Patient: “I know that my dad has… I think it's hypothyroidism… he's got some autoimmune stuff going on, like that much I know.” This matches hypothyroidism/autoimmune condition.
Patient: “my mom… she's got diabetes type two. She's got hypertension… she's got high cholesterol.” This corresponds to type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.

Patient: “I've started taking this boxing class. I've been taking this boxing class for a few weeks… I work out… and I… don't really have any medical problems.” This supports regular boxing and general regular exercise.

Patient describes a binge episode: “we were like out partying until… late hours, and I just got uncharacteristically drunk for me.” While baseline frequency of alcohol use is not detailed, a recent binge drinking episode is clearly reported, supporting “social alcohol consumer; recent binge drinking noted” as a reasonable inference.
Doctor: “Do you wear glasses at all, glasses, contact lenses?” Patient: “No. No, so no glasses.” This supports that she does not wear glasses or contacts.

Doctor suspects central demyelination (MS): “sometimes you know you do get things like MS… people… can have visual problems… and… numbness tingling…” but no explicit mention of a peripheral or cervical etiology is made. The added consideration of a peripheral/cervical cause is not stated in the transcript.

Doctor links symptoms to possible MS but does not specifically name optic neuritis: “people with multiple sclerosis can have, um, visual problems, like what you've experienced…” The term “optic neuritis” and explicit interpretation of the event as such are not mentioned.

Patient reacts with clear anxiety: “Ohh my God! Will I be in a wheelchair?” Doctor also notes: “I know this might sound a bit of a shock to you… I do appreciate you are a bit worried.” This supports that she is anxious about the potential diagnosis.

Doctor: “I'm going to do an urgent, very urgent neurology referral… What that might entail is the brain scan and things like that.” This supports an urgent neurology referral for MRI brain and full neurological work‑up; spine is not explicitly mentioned but is a reasonable extension of “brain scan and things like that.”

Doctor: “while you're waiting… if there's any weakness… progresses to your legs, or there's any kind of headaches, vomiting, fits, and your visual symptoms are getting worse and not getting better, then that would be an A and E.” This matches education on red‑flag symptoms (progressive weakness, visual loss, headache, vomiting, seizures) and instruction to attend A&E.

Doctor states no disease‑specific treatment yet: “that's something we can't do… first we need to firm diagnosis.” However, he does not explicitly advise to ‘continue ibuprofen as needed’; ibuprofen use is described by the patient but no continuation instruction is given.

Doctor provides verbal reassurance: “I know this might sound a bit of a shock to you… it's good that… you've come… and hopefully we'll get things sorted and the ball rolling.” While specific “support resources” are not named, the offer of reassurance and supportive conversation pending specialist review is evident.
